name: Daria Yilmaz

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: I'm with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to employers or AI companies. Your answers are confidential. What does a normal working day look like?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I give beginner guitar lessons at the community centre, copy simple parts and clean up demo recordings when there is time. I play rhythm guitar for a Saturday band, and I still have to practise the harder songs after the children are asleep.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: What is the household carrying right now?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: Eli works in a hotel kitchen and we have two school-age children and a mortgage. I left school after secondary classes, am still a junior musician, and have less than a month's expenses saved.

say: I would tell parents that **beginner lessons** still need a patient player beside their children.
I would accept **quicker lesson sheets** without expecting a new way of earning.
think: The **mortgage** worries me now because centre hours are offered only term by term.
Eli's **kitchen pay** buys groceries, but we have less than one month's savings.
do: Ask the **centre manager** for next term's lesson hours in writing this week.
Keep my **four pupils** and confirmed Saturday band dates.
Put **twenty** from two paid Saturdays toward the mortgage instead of buying a pedal.
feel: I feel **anxious** about a cancelled term and the mortgage.
S0.quote: A mild AI story doesn't change the date on our mortgage bill.
fieldNote: Her **term-by-term hours** and thin savings make the baseline job insecure.
She has used **hotel cleanup shifts** before and would call the lender early if lessons vanished.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the centre parents that a quicker lesson sheet is fine, but their children still need someone to keep time beside them. The Saturday band will still have to carry its own gear into the hall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'm already counting the mortgage days even before AI comes up. My partner Eli's hotel kitchen pay covers groceries, but I have less than a month's expenses put by and the centre only books me term by term.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll keep my four beginner guitar pupils and ask the centre manager for next term's hours in writing this week. If the band pays for two Saturdays, I'll put twenty aside toward the mortgage instead of buying another pedal.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious because one cancelled term could leave us behind on the loan. A mild AI story doesn't change the date on our mortgage bill.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What did one lost pupil mean at home?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Last term one family stopped lessons without notice, and I lost the money for the school shoes. I took an extra kitchen cleanup shift with Eli's hotel for two evenings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Which call would you make before missing the mortgage?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd call the lender before the mortgage date if a centre term vanished. I'd rather ask about a payment arrangement early than hide the letter from Eli.

do: Request the **spring timetable** and attend the association with my hours list this month.
Apply for **library shelving** if a vacancy opens after more than one lesson day is cut.
Keep **weekend gigs** while looking for replacement hours.
feel: I feel **alarmed** because one lost paid day threatens the mortgage.
S1.quote: A meeting alone won't pay the mortgage, but silence won't protect our lesson hours.
fieldNote: She sees **thinking tasks** eating into a junior musician's paid centre hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the other centre tutors to keep a record of the hours software replaces. If the centre saves money on booking and practice sheets, it should tell us where the remaining paid hours go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I do basic demo edits, lesson sheets and bookings, and that is almost half my centre time. I am still learning guitar myself, so I can't assume parents will pay extra for my lessons when a cheap tool gives feedback.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This month I'll ask the centre for its proposed spring timetable and attend the musicians association meeting with my hours list. In the first year of change, if the centre cuts more than one lesson day, I'll apply for the part-time library shelving post if it opens and keep weekend gigs.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed because a lost lesson day would hit the mortgage before I could build savings. A meeting alone won't pay the mortgage, but silence won't protect our lesson hours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who would you take the hours question to?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: There are three tutors on my corridor and one already lost a Thursday slot. I would ask for the change in writing before we take it to the association.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Is the library work actually available?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The library posted a shelving job last summer, but it may not open again. I'd ask about the next vacancy rather than tell Eli I have a job waiting.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the tutors that full AGI by 2028 means we must ask about hours now. I would still turn up for Saturday gigs while the band has paying rooms.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AGI in 2028 could write lesson plans, edit demos and teach practice exercises cheaper than I can. Robot players might come around 2031, but my screen and teaching hours could fall first. My partner's kitchen wage will not cover the mortgage alone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This week I'll list every centre hour and ask the manager for a written autumn schedule. In the first year after 2028, if my centre hours halve, I'll ask the hotel about two cleanup shifts and contact the lender about temporary payment terms before a bill is late.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel alarmed and close to the edge, but I can make those calls. We have almost no spare month to wait for a better music job nearby.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the hotel definitely take you back?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The hotel gave me two cleanup evenings once, but I cannot count on another offer. I would take shifts only if the supervisor confirms openings and the hours do not clash with the pupils I still have.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you ask the lender before changing payments?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would ask the lender what a temporary change costs in interest. I don't want a smaller bill now to turn into a larger debt later without understanding it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the centre tutors five years gives us time to ask for training while we still have hours. I would rather teach children to play together than compete with a machine over printed exercises.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: AGI in 2031 could do my lesson plans and demo editing, with robot players around 2034. Five years might let me qualify as a classroom music aide, but I have only secondary school behind me and cannot pay course fees from our mortgage money.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Next term I'll ask the adult college about its classroom aide course and apply only if a grant covers the fee and the timetable fits my centre work. Before 2031 I'll seek a school placement if I complete the course; in the first year after AGI, I'll apply for an aide post if one opens and keep weekend band work.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious because there's time for a course, but no money to waste on the wrong one. Eli and I would need to plan childcare around the evening classes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Who watches the children during evening classes?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The younger child is nine and needs someone home on Tuesdays. Eli could cover only if the hotel gives an earlier shift, so I'd ask before registering.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How would you know the certificate helps?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would check whether schools nearby actually accept the certificate. If they do not, I won't borrow money for a paper that changes nothing. A certificate is no use if the school won't hire the person holding it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell the band a decade is time to build a life with steadier work beside music. I would still play for our neighbours if they want the sound of us in the hall.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'll be 53 when AGI arrives in 2036, with robot players possibly around 2039. I cannot wait for retirement; I need the mortgage paid well before then, and basic editing fees could fade long before full AGI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: This year I'll ask the local school about aide requirements and enrol in a funded course if it is required and the classes fit childcare. By 2036 I'll try to hold regular school hours alongside band dates; in the first year after AGI, I'll keep lessons only if families still pay and the school timetable permits them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I feel anxious even with time to ask about school work. A ten-year warning still comes with twelve mortgage bills each year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: When would you leave the centre for a school post?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I would not quit the centre on a promise from a school. I would wait for a written offer and make sure the new pay covers mortgage and travel.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would older children change the budget?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If our youngest reaches adulthood by then, childcare costs may ease. I cannot spend that possible saving today, so I'll keep a record of what the household actually spends.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: AGI by 2028 worries me most because centre hours could halve before I can replace them, and Eli cannot cover the mortgage alone. Written hours, confirmed hotel shifts if they exist, and clear lender terms would help us avoid arrears.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask who carries the children when a worker takes evening training. A free course isn't free to our household if my partner loses a shift to watch the children.

headlineQuote: A free course isn't free to our household if my partner loses a shift to watch the children.
portrait: Daria is a **43-year-old** junior musician with secondary education, teaching beginner guitar, editing demos and playing rhythm guitar.
She and Eli have **two children**, a mortgage and less than a month's savings; his hotel pay covers groceries.
Her **centre hours** include thinking tasks exposed before robot players arrive three years after AGI.
She seeks **written hours**, conditional hotel shifts, lender terms and funded training that fits childcare.
biggestWorry: **AGI by 2028** worries her most because centre hours could halve before replacement work appears.
whatWouldHelp: Written **centre hours**, available hotel shifts and clear lender terms would help the household avoid mortgage arrears.
